newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO urges expatriates to invest in West Bank, Gaza.
newsitem.headline: PLO urges expatriates to invest in West Bank, Gaza.

text.p: The Palestinian Authority on Monday urged expatriate Palestinians to invest in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
But businessmen complained Israeli restrictions and poor Palestinian investment laws were choking the private sector.

"Palestinian hands, capital and brains which succeeded so well to build other Arab states should return," Palestinian Finance Minister Mohammed Zuhdi al-Nashashibi told a conference of businessmen from the Palestinian diaspora.
"We want to end the situation of dependency that was created by the occupiers," Nashashibi said in PLO-ruled Gaza.

The PLO has long hoped the capital and human resources of Palestinian expatriates, dispersed by Middle East wars across the Arab world, North America and Europe, would stream back to the homeland following Israeli-PLO peace deals.

But private investors have mainly remained on the sidelines as hopes of an economic "peace dividend" dwindled in the face of extended Israeli closures of the West Bank and Gaza, political volatility and PLO governmental inexperience.
"Local marketing capability is limited because the world is closed to Gaza and the West Bank," Talat Othman, a Chicago-based financial consultant born in the West Bank, told the conference.
"It is impossible for Palestinian business to provide a reliable business schedule...the economy is captive," he said.

Some 90 percent of Palestinian trade flows to or through Israel, which occupied the West Bank and Gaza in 1967. Tight Israeli security checks and periodic closures imposed to keep out Arab militants have wreaked economic havoc in the area.
The opening of new Gaza air and sea ports have been bogged down in a four-month crisis in Israeli-PLO peace talks.
"If the Palestinians are given the opportunity to compete in a level playing field I have no doubt that they will succeed in trade competition," Othman said.

Samir Abdullah, chief of the Palestine Arab Investment Bank, said Palestinian private investment last year stood at $300 million, compared to the Palestinian Authority's 1997 budget of $866 million and the $1.4 billion world donors have supplied since 1993.
"Palestinian private absorption capacity stands at $2 billion a year. Our diaspora resources far exceed that," Abdullah told Reuters.
But he and many other businessmen said a lack of transparent investment laws impeded private sector activity.
"We need modern laws to stimulate private sector development...the Palestinian Authority has not done 10 percent what it could have done," Abdullah said.
Expatriate businessmen nonetheless expressed optimism the West Bank and Gaza, poor in resources but rich in human capital, could provide sound investment opportunities.
"When the risk is greater, the opportunities are greater," Mahmoud al-Farra, whose al-Farra Group holds $70 million in industrial, banking and consulting interests, told Reuters.
Chicago dentist Mohammad Khalil Salih said he was building business ties so he could relocate to the West Bank.
"I'm still optimistic. There is a light at the end of the tunnel. We will get there. If everything is given to us on a silver platter it won't be fun," Salih told Reuters.
